Unique ergodicity for a class of stochastic hyperbolic equations with additive space-time white noise
Leonardo Tolomeo

Abstract
In this paper, we consider a certain class of second order nonlinear PDEs with damping and space-time white noise forcing, posed on the d d -dimensional torus. This class includes the wave equation for d = 1 d=1 and the beam equation for d ≤ 3 d\leq 3 . We show that the Gibbs measure is the unique invariant measure for this system. Since the flow does not satisfy the Strong Feller property, we introduce a new technique for showing unique ergodicity. This approach may be also useful in situations in which finite-time blowup is possible.

1
Introduction

Consider the equation

u_{tt}+u_{t}+u+(-\Delta)^{\frac{s}{2}}u+u^{3}=\sqrt{2}\xi,

posed on the
d
- dimensional torus
\mathbb{T}^{d}
, where
\xi
is the
space-time white noise
on
\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{T}^{d}
(defined in Section 2), and
s>d
.

By expressing this equation in vectorial notation,

\partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
1+(-\Delta)^{\frac{s}{2}}&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{3}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0\\
\sqrt{2}\xi\end{pmatrix},

(1)

from a formal computation, we expect this system to preserve
the
Gibbs
measure

\mathrm{d}\rho(u,u_{t})``="\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int u^{4}-\frac{1}{2}\int u^{2}+|(-\Delta)^{\frac{s}{2}}u|^{2}\Big)\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\int u_{t}^{2}\Big)``\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}u_{t}",

where
``\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}u_{t}"
is the non-existent Lebesgue measure on an infinite dimensional vector space (of functions).
Heuristically,
we expect invariance for this measure by splitting (
1
) into

1.

\partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
1+(-\Delta)^{\frac{s}{2}}&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{3}\end{pmatrix},

which is a Hamiltonian PDE in the variables
u,u_{t}
, and so it should preserve
the Gibbs measure

\exp\Big(-H(u,u_{t})\Big)``\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}u_{t}",

where
H(u,u_{t})=\frac{1}{4}\int u^{4}+\frac{1}{2}\int u^{2}+|(-\Delta)^{\frac{s}{2}}u|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int u_{t}^{2}
,

2.

\partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\
\sqrt{2}\xi\end{pmatrix},

which is the Ornstein - Uhlenbeck process in the variable
u_{t}
, and so it preserves the spatial white noise

\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\int u_{t}^{2}\Big)``\mathrm{d}u_{t}".

For
s=1
, up to the damping term
\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\int u_{t}^{2}\Big)\mathrm{d}u_{t}
, the measure
\rho
corresponds to the well known
\Phi^{4}_{d}
model of quantum field theory,
which is known to be definable without resorting to renormalisation just for
d=1
(this measure will be rigorously defined - in the case
s>d
- in Section 2).

Our goal is to study the global behaviour of the flow of (
1
),
by proving invariance of the measure
\rho
and furthermore showing that
\rho
is the unique invariant measure for the flow.

Following ideas first appearing in Bourgain’s seminal paper
[
1
]
and in the works of McKean-Vasinski
[
33
]
and McKean
[
34
,
35
]
, there have been many
developments in proving invariance of the Gibbs measure for
deterministic
dispersive PDEs (see for instance

[
2
,
3
,
4
,
5
,
6
,
7
,
9
,
25
,
38
,
39
,
40
]
).

A natural question that arises when an invariant measure is present is uniqueness of the invariant measure and convergence to equilibrium starting from a “good enough” initial data. This has been extensively studied in
the case of parabolic stochastic PDEs (see for instance
[
12
,
13
,
16
,
19
,
20
,
24
,
41
,
45
]
and references therein) and for stochastic equations coming from fluid dynamics (see
[
14
,
23
,
46
]
and references therein).
On the other hand, there are not many results in the dispersive setting, and they often rely either on some smoother version of the noise
\xi
, or onto some dissipative properties of the system (see for instance
[
15
,
21
,
26
,
28
,
29
,
27
,
30
,
31
,
32
,
36
]
).
Indeed, as far as the author knows, the ergodicity result of this paper is the first that can deal with a forcing as rough as space-time white noise in a setting without any dissipation. More precisely, we will prove the following:

Theorem 1.1
.

Let
s=4,d=3
. Then the measure
\rho
is invariant for the Markov process associated to the flow
\Phi_{t}(\cdot,\xi)
of (
1
), in the sense that for every
function
F
measurable and bounded, for
{\mathbf{u}}=(u,u_{t})^{\textup{T}}
,

\int\mathbb{E}[F(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}},\xi))]\mathrm{d}\rho({\mathbf{u}})=\int F({\mathbf{u}})\mathrm{d}\rho({\mathbf{u}})\text{ for every }t>0.

(2)

Moreover, there exists a Banach space
X^{\alpha}
which contains the Sobolev Space
\mathcal{H}^{\frac{s}{2}}:=H^{\frac{s}{2}}\times L^{2}
, such that for every
0<\alpha<\frac{s-d}{2}
,
\rho
is the only invariant measure concentrated on
X^{\alpha}
. Furthermore, for every
{\mathbf{u}}_{0}\in X^{\alpha}
and for every
F:X^{\alpha}\to\mathbb{R}
continuous and bounded,

\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbb{E}[F(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0},\xi))]\mathrm{d}t=\int F({\mathbf{u}})\mathrm{d}\rho(u).

(3)

We will carry out the proof in full details only in the case
s=4,d=3
, however the same proof can be extended to the general nonsingular case
s>d
. We will describe in more details how to obtain the general result in Section 1.4.

The proof of this theorem is heavily influenced by the recent parabolic literature, and in particular by results that use or are inspired by the Bismut-Elworthy-Li formula, especially
[
45
]
and
[
24
]
.
A crucial step in these papers is showing that the flow of the equation in study satisfies the Strong Feller property. However, as we will prove in Section 5, the flow of
(
1
) does
not

satisfy the Strong Feller property, therefore a more refined approach is needed.

While the argument in this work does not provide any information on the rate of convergence to equilibrium,
it does not rely on good long time estimates, as opposed to works that rely on the
Asymptotic Strong Feller
property defined in
[
22
]
. In particular, as far as ergodicity is concerned
(in the sense that (
3
) holds
\rho
-a.s.),
we use just the qualitative result of global existence of the flow, and it may be possible to extend this approach even to situations in which finite-time blowup is possible, similarly to the result in
[
24
]
. This goes in the direction of dealing with the
singular
case
s=d
. Indeed, in the case
s=d=2
, in a upcoming work by M.Gubinelli, H. Koch, T. Oh and the author, we prove global well posedness and invariance of the Gibbs measure for the renormalised damped wave equation

u_{tt}+u_{t}+u-\Delta u+:\hskip-2.0pt{u^{3}}\hskip-2.0pt:=\sqrt{2}\xi.

See also
[
43
,
44
]
for the global existence part of the argument.

However, since the best bound available with the argument grows more than exponentially in time, any approach on unique ergodicity that relies on good long time estimate has little chance to yield any result for this equation.

1.1
Structure of the argument and organisation of the paper

In order to make this paper less notation-heavy, we will concentrate on the case
d=3
,
s=4
, which is the Beam equation in 3-d

\partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
1+\Delta^{2}&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{3}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0\\
\sqrt{2}\xi\end{pmatrix}.\\

(4)

Local and global well posedness for the non-damped version of this equation have been explored in detail in an upcoming work by R. Mosincat, O. Pocovnicu, the author, and Y. Wang (see also
[
43
]
). We will however present an independent treatment that works for general
s>d
.
While the case
s=2,d=1
, which corresponds to wave equation in 1 dimension, can arguably be considered more interesting, we decide to focus on (
4
) because it presents all the difficulties of the general case (namely, the definition of the spaces
X^{\alpha}
, and some subtleties that come from the multidimensional nature of the equation). At the end of this section, we will discuss how to convert the proof for this case into the proof for the general case.

The paper and the proof of Theorem
1.1
are organised as follows:

•

4
), and introduce the spaces

as well as define rigorously the measure
\rho
and prove the related
X^{\alpha}
estimates for a generic initial data sampled according to
\rho
.

•

In Section 3, we build the flow, by showing local and global well posedness of the equation (
4
). Local well posedness is shown by applying a standard Banach fixed point argument, after reformulating the equation
using the so-called Da Prato-Debussche trick. Global well posedness is shown via an energy estimate, making use of an integration by parts trick similar to the one used in
[
37
]
.

•

In Section 4, we show invariance for the measure
\rho
.

•

Section 5 is dedicated to showing unique ergodicity of
\rho
. In particular, we first recover the Strong Feller
property by changing the underlying topology of the space
X^{\alpha}
. However, with this new topology, the space ceases to be connected and separable. Therefore, even when we combine this property with irreducibility of the flow, we derive just the partial information that if
\rho_{1}\perp\rho_{2}
are invariant, then there exists a Borel set
V
s.t.

\rho_{1}(V+\mathcal{H}^{2})=0,\rho_{2}(V+\mathcal{H}^{2})=1.

In order to obtain ergodicity of
\rho
, we combine this argument with a completely algebraic one. We consider the projection
\pi:X^{\alpha}\to X^{\alpha}/\mathcal{H}^{\frac{s}{2}}
, and we show that if
\rho_{1},\rho_{2}\ll\rho
, then
\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{1}=\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{2}=\pi_{\sharp}\rho
, which contradicts the existence of such
V
.

Finally, to conclude uniqueness, we show that for every
{\mathbf{u}}_{0}\in X^{\alpha}
, if
\mu_{t}
is the law of

{\mathbf{u}}(t)=(u(t),u_{t}(t))
, then every weak limit
\nu
of
\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mu_{t}\mathrm{d}t
will satisfy
\pi_{\sharp}\nu=\pi_{\sharp}\rho
, from which we derive
\nu=\rho
.

1.2
Mild formulation

Before discussing ergodicity issues, we need to define the flow of (
4
). Consider the
linear
damped beam equation with forcing
\mathbf{f}=\begin{pmatrix}f\\
g\end{pmatrix}
and initial data

{\mathbf{u}}_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\
u_{1}\end{pmatrix}
,

\partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
1+\Delta^{2}&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}f\\
g\end{pmatrix}.

By variation of constants, the solution to this equation is given by

{\mathbf{u}}=S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}S(t-t^{\prime})\mathbf{f}(t^{\prime})\mathrm{d}t^{\prime},

(5)

where
S(t)
is the operator formally defined as

e^{-\frac{t}{2}}\resizebox{20348790}{}{$\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\cos\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\Delta^{2}}\Big)+\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sin\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\Delta^{2}}\Big)}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\Delta^{2}}}&\frac{\sin\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\Delta^{2}}\Big)}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\Delta^{2}}}\\
-\Big(\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\Delta^{2}}-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\Delta^{2}}}\Big)\sin\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\Delta^{2}}\Big)&\cos\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\Delta^{2}}\Big)-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sin\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\Delta^{2}}\Big)}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+\Delta^{2}}}\end{pmatrix}$},

or equivalently, is the operator that corresponds to the symbol

e^{-\frac{t}{2}}\resizebox{20348790}{}{$\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\cos\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}\Big)+\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sin\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}\Big)}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}}&\frac{\sin\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}\Big)}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}}\\
-\Big(\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}}\Big)\sin\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}\Big)&\cos\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}\Big)-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sin\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}\Big)}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}}\end{pmatrix}$}

in Fourier series. We notice that this operator maps distributions to distributions, and for every
\alpha\in\mathbb{R}
,
it maps the Sobolev space
\mathcal{H}^{\alpha}:=H^{\alpha}\times H^{\alpha-2}
into itself, with
the estimate
\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{\alpha}}\lesssim e^{-\frac{t}{2}}\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{\alpha}}
.

By the formula
(
5
), since we formally have
\mathbf{f}=-\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{3}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0\\
\xi\end{pmatrix}
, we expect the solution of
(
4
) to satisfy the
Duhamel
formulation

{\mathbf{u}}=S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{0}+\int_{0}^{t}S(t-t^{\prime})\begin{pmatrix}0\\
\xi(t^{\prime})\end{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}-\int_{0}^{t}S(t-t^{\prime})\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{3}(t^{\prime})\end{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}t^{\prime}.

(6)

From the previous discussion about
S(t)
, we have that

\lxSVG@closescope }
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}_{t}(\xi)+{\mathbf{v}}(t)\in X
as well.
Due to the dispersive nature of the equation, this choice is not as straightforward as in the parabolic case,
where Hölder spaces satisfy all of the required properties. On the other hand, keeping track only of the
\mathcal{H}^{\alpha}
regularity of the initial data would hide important information about the solution, namely the gain in regularity of the term
{\mathbf{v}}
. A good space for this equation turns out to be

\begin{gathered}\overline{X}^{\alpha}:=\big\{{\mathbf{u}}\in S^{\prime}(\mathbb{T}^{d})\times S^{\prime}(\mathbb{T}^{d})|S(t){\mathbf{u}}\in C([0,+\infty);\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}),\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}\lesssim e^{-\frac{t}{8}}\big\},\\
\left\|{u}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}:=\sup_{t\geq 0}e^{\frac{t}{8}}\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}},\end{gathered}

for
0<\alpha<\frac{1}{2}
.
Here
\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}:=C^{\alpha}\times C^{\alpha-2}
. As it is common in these situations, the particular definition
of the Hölder spaces
C^{\beta}
for
\beta\not\in(0,1)
(where they all coincide) does not play any role. In this paper,
we choose to define
\left\|{u}\right\|_{C^{\beta}}:=\left\|{(1-\Delta)^{\frac{\beta}{2}}u}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}
.

As it is defined, the space
\overline{X}^{\alpha}
might not be separable, which is a helpful hypothesis for some measure theoretical considerations in the following. In order to solve this issue, we will denote by
X^{\alpha}
the closure of trigonometric
polynomials in
\overline{X}^{\alpha}
. Since we have, for
\alpha^{\prime}>\alpha
,

\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}-P_{\leq N}{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}\lesssim N^{-\frac{\alpha^{\prime}-\alpha}{2}}\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha^{\prime}}},

we have that for every
\alpha^{\prime}>\alpha
, if
\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha^{\prime}}}<+\infty
, then
{\mathbf{u}}\in X^{\alpha}
.

Lemma 1.2
.

\overline{X}^{\alpha}
is a Banach space.

Proof.

\left\|{\cdot}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}
is clearly a norm, so we just need to show completeness. Let
{\mathbf{u}}_{n}
be a Cauchy sequence in
\overline{X}^{\alpha}
. By definition, for every
t
,
S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}
is a Cauchy sequence in
\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}
, so there exists a limit
S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}\to{\mathbf{u}}(t)
in
\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}
. Moreover,

S(t)
is a bounded operator in
\mathcal{H}^{\alpha}
, so one has that

{\mathbf{u}}(t)=\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}-\lim S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}=\mathcal{H}^{\alpha}-\lim S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}=S(t)(\mathcal{H}^{\alpha}-\lim{\mathbf{u}}_{n})=S(t){\mathbf{u}}(0).

Lastly,

\displaystyle\lim_{n}\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}_{n}-{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}

\displaystyle=\lim_{n}\sup_{t}e^{\frac{t}{8}}\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}-S(t){\mathbf{u}}(0)}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}

\displaystyle=\lim_{n}\sup_{t}\lim_{m}e^{\frac{t}{8}}\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}-S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{m}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}

\displaystyle\leq\lim_{n}\lim_{m}\sup_{t}e^{\frac{t}{8}}\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}-S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{m}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}

\displaystyle=\lim_{n}\lim_{m}\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}_{n}-{\mathbf{u}}_{m}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}

\displaystyle=0.

∎

Since the operator
S(t)
is
not
bounded on
\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}
, the space
X^{\alpha}
might appear
mysterious. However, in the next sections, we will see that the term

belongs to
X^{\alpha}
, as well as almost every initial data according to
\rho
, i.e.
\rho(X^{\alpha})=~1
. Moreover, we have the following embedding for smooth functions:

Lemma 1.3
.

For every
0<\alpha<\frac{1}{2}
, we have
\mathcal{H}^{2}\subset X^{\alpha}
. Moreover, the identity

\id:\mathcal{H}^{2}\hookrightarrow X^{\alpha}
is a compact operator.

Proof.

Let
{\mathbf{u}}\in\mathcal{H}^{2}
. By Sobolev embeddings,

\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}\lesssim\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\lesssim e^{-\frac{t}{2}}\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}

and given
s\geq 0
, we have

\lim_{t\to s}\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}-S(s){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}\lesssim\limsup_{t\to s}\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}-S(s){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}=0,

hence
{\mathbf{u}}\in X^{\alpha}
.

Now let
{\mathbf{u}}_{n}
be a bounded sequence in
\mathcal{H}^{2}
. By compactness of Sobolev embeddings, up to
subsequences,
{\mathbf{u}}_{n}\to{\mathbf{u}}
in
\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}
and
{\mathbf{u}}_{n}\rightharpoonup{\mathbf{u}}
weakly in
\mathcal{H}^{s}
for every
s\leq 2
. Therefore,

S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}\rightharpoonup S(t){\mathbf{u}}
weakly in
\mathcal{H}^{s}
for every
t\geq 0
.

By a diagonal argument, up to subsequences, we have that
S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}
is a converging sequence in
\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}
for every
t\in\mathbb{Q}^{+}
, so by coherence of the limits,
S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}\to S(t){\mathbf{u}}
in
\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}

for every
t\in\mathbb{Q}^{+}
. By the property

\partial_{t}S(t)=-\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
1+\Delta^{2}&1\end{pmatrix}S(t),

we have that
\left\|{{S(t){\mathbf{u}}-S(s)}{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s}}\lesssim|t-s|^{\varepsilon}\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{s+4\varepsilon}}
. Therefore,
by taking
\varepsilon
such that
\alpha+4\varepsilon+\frac{3}{2}<2
, by the Sobolev embedding

\mathcal{H}^{2-4\varepsilon}\hookrightarrow\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}
, we have that

S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}\to S(t){\mathbf{u}}
in
\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}
for every
t\geq 0
and uniformly on compact sets. Finally, for every
T
we have

\displaystyle e^{\frac{t}{8}}\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}-S(t){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}\lesssim e^{\frac{T}{8}}\sup_{s\in[0,T]}\left\|{S(s){\mathbf{u}}_{n}-S(s){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}+e^{-\frac{3}{8}T}\sup_{n}\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}_{n}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}.

For
T\gg 1
big enough and
n\gg 1
(depending on
T
), we can make the right hand side arbitrarily small. Therefore, we get
\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}_{n}-{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}\to 0
as
n\to\infty
, so
\id
is compact.
∎

However, the space
X^{\alpha}
is strictly bigger than
\mathcal{H}^{2}
, and it contains functions at regularity exactly
\alpha
. Indeed, we have

Lemma 1.4
.

For every
\alpha_{1}>\alpha>0
, there exists
{\mathbf{u}}_{0}\in X^{\alpha}
such that
{\mathbf{u}}_{0}\not\in\mathcal{H}^{\alpha_{1}}
.

Proof.

Suppose by contradiction that
X^{\alpha}\subseteq\mathcal{H}^{\alpha_{1}}
. By the closed graph theorem, this implies that

\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{\alpha_{1}}}\lesssim\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}.

(8)

For
n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}
, consider
{\mathbf{u}}_{n}:=\begin{pmatrix}e^{in\cdot x}\\
0\end{pmatrix}
. By definition of
S(t)
,

S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}=e^{-\frac{t}{2}}\begin{pmatrix}\left(\cos\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}\Big)+\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sin\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}\Big)}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}}\right)e^{in\cdot x}\\
\frac{\sin\Big(t\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}\Big)}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}+|n|^{4}}}e^{in\cdot x}\end{pmatrix}.

It is easy to check that
\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}\sim e^{-\frac{t}{2}}\left\langle{n}\right\rangle^{\alpha}
, so
\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{n}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}\sim\left\langle{n}\right\rangle^{\alpha}
.
On the other hand,
\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}_{n}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{\alpha_{1}}}\sim\left\langle{n}\right\rangle^{\alpha_{1}}
. By (
8
), this implies
\left\langle{n}\right\rangle^{\alpha_{1}}\lesssim\left\langle{n}\right\rangle^{\alpha}
, which is a contradiction.
∎

1.3
Truncated system

In order to prove invariance of the measure
\mu
, it will be helpful to introduce a truncated system. While
many truncations are possible, for this particular class of systems it is helpful to introduce the sharp
Fourier truncation
P_{\leq N}
,
N\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}
given by

P_{\leq N}{\mathbf{u}}(x):=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3}}\sum_{\max_{j}{|n_{j}|}\leq N}\widehat{{\mathbf{u}}}(n)e^{in\cdot x},

i.e. the sharp restriction on the cube
[-N,N]^{3}
in Fourier variable. Similarly, we define

P_{>N}:=1-P_{\leq N}
. While this is a somewhat odd choice for the truncation, it has the advantages that

P_{>N}
and
P_{\leq N}
have orthogonal ranges, and

\left\|{P_{\leq N}u}\right\|_{L^{p}}\lesssim_{p}\left\|{u}\right\|_{L^{p}}
uniformly in
N
for every
1<p<+\infty
(since it corresponds to the composition of the Hilbert transform in every variable).

It is convenient for notation to allow also
N=-1
, in which case
P_{\leq N}=0
and
P_{>N}=\id
. Therefore,
we define the
truncated
system to be

\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}&=&-\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
1+\Delta^{2}&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}-P_{\leq N}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
(P_{\leq N}u)^{3}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0\\
\sqrt{2}\xi\end{pmatrix},\\
&\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}(0)&=&\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\
u_{1}\end{pmatrix}\in X^{\alpha}.\end{aligned}\right.

(9)

4
), we will write solutions to this system as

(10)

1.4
Notation and conversion to the general case

In the following,
\mathcal{H}^{\alpha}
will denote the Sobolev space
H^{\alpha}\times H^{\alpha-2}
, with norm given by

\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{\alpha}}^{2}:=\left\|{(1-\Delta)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}u}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\left\|{(1-\Delta)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}-1}u_{t}}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.

Similarly,
\mathscr{W}^{\alpha,p}
will denote the Sobolev space
W^{\alpha,p}\times W^{\alpha-2,p}
with norm given by

\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathscr{W}^{\alpha}}^{p}:=\left\|{(1-\Delta)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}u}\right\|_{L^{p}}^{p}+\left\|{(1-\Delta)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}-1}u_{t}}\right\|_{L^{p}}^{p}

and as already discussed,
\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}:=C^{\alpha}\times C^{\alpha-2}
, with norm given by

\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}:=\max\left(\left\|{(1-\Delta)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}u}\right\|_{L^{\infty}},\left\|{(1-\Delta)^{\frac{\alpha}{2}-1}u_{t}}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}\right).

In order to convert the argument presented in this paper into the one for the general case, we make the following modifications:

\mathcal{H}^{\alpha}:=H^{\alpha}\times H^{\alpha-\frac{s}{2}},\hskip 6.0pt\mathscr{W}^{\alpha,p}=W^{\alpha,p}\times W^{\alpha-\frac{s}{2},p},\hskip 6.0pt\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}:=C^{\alpha}\times C^{\alpha-\frac{s}{2}},

with the analogous modifications of the norms. Moreover,
S(t)
would denote the linear propagator for (
1
), and

\begin{gathered}\overline{X}^{\alpha}:=\big\{{\mathbf{u}}|S(t){\mathbf{u}}\in C([0,+\infty);\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}),\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}\lesssim e^{-\frac{t}{8}}\big\},\\
\left\|{u}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}:=\sup_{t>0}e^{\frac{t}{8}}\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}\end{gathered}

is defined for
0<\alpha<\frac{s-d}{2}
.
Moreover, in the following discussion, the space
\mathcal{H}^{2}
has to be substituted by the space
\mathcal{H}^{\frac{s}{2}}
, and
any threshold of the regularity in the form
\alpha<\frac{1}{2}
has to be substituted by
\alpha<\frac{s-d}{2}
.

2.1
Stochastic convolution

We will use that the space-time white noise is a distribution-valued random variable such that, for every

\phi,\psi\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{T}^{d})
,

\mathbb{E}[\left\langle\phi,\xi\right\rangle\left\langle\psi,\xi\right\rangle]=\left\langle\phi,\psi\right\rangle_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{T}^{d})}.

.

\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{t}\left\langle S(t-t^{\prime})\begin{pmatrix}0\\

\displaystyle=\sqrt{2}\left\langle\xi,\pi_{2}S(t-t^{\prime})^{\ast}\mathbf{f}\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}},

where
\pi_{2}
is the projection on the second component. Therefore, by definition of
\xi
,

\gamma(t,s)[\mathbf{f}]=2\int_{0}^{t\wedge s}\left\langle\Re\big(\pi_{2}S(t-t^{\prime})^{\ast}\mathbf{f}\big),\Re\big(\pi_{2}S(s-t^{\prime})^{\ast}\mathbf{f}\big)\right\rangle.

(12)

Hence, by boundedness of
S(t)
, we have that
\gamma(t,s)[\mathbf{f}]\lesssim\left\|{f}\right\|_{H^{-2}}^{2}+\left\|{f_{t}}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}
. Moreover,
since

\partial_{t}S(t)=-\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
1+\Delta^{2}&1\end{pmatrix}S(t),

we have
\Lip(\gamma(\cdot,\cdot)[\mathbf{f}])\lesssim\left\|{f}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\left\|{f_{t}}\right\|_{H^{2}}^{2}
, so by interpolation, for every
0\leq\theta\leq 1
, we have

\big|\gamma(t,s)-\gamma(t^{\prime},s^{\prime})\big|[\mathbf{f}]\lesssim(\left\|{f}\right\|_{H^{-2(1+\theta)}}^{2}+\left\|{f_{t}}\right\|_{H^{2\theta}}^{2})(|t-t^{\prime}|+|s-s^{\prime}|)^{\theta}.

2.2
Invariant measure

Consider the distribution-valued random variable

{\mathbf{u}}=\begin{pmatrix}\Re\Big(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\frac{g_{n}}{\sqrt{1+|n|^{4}}}e^{inx}\Big)\\
\Re\Big(\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}h_{n}e^{inx}\Big)\end{pmatrix}

(15)

where
g_{n},h_{n}
are independent complex-valued standard gaussians (i.e. the real and imaginary parts are independent real valued standard gaussians). If
\mathbf{f}=\begin{pmatrix}f\\
f_{t}\end{pmatrix}
is a test function, then

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\left\langle{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{f}\right\rangle^{2}]

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n}\frac{\mathbb{E}|g_{n}|^{2}}{1+|n|^{4}}|\hat{f}(n)|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n}\mathbb{E}|h_{n}|^{2}|\hat{f}_{t}(n)|^{2}

(16)

\displaystyle=\sum_{n}\frac{|\hat{f}(n)|^{2}}{1+|n|^{4}}+\sum_{n}|\hat{f}_{t}(n)|^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\|{(1+\Delta^{2})^{-\frac{1}{2}}f}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\left\|{f_{t}}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.

Therefore, if
\mu
is the law of
{\mathbf{u}}
, we have that formally

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}})

\displaystyle=\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\left\|{(1+\Delta^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}u}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)\mathrm{d}u\,\times\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\left\|{u_{t}}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\Big)\mathrm{d}u_{t}

(17)

\displaystyle=\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\int u^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int(\Delta u)^{2}\Big)\mathrm{d}u\,\times\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\int u_{t}^{2}\Big)\mathrm{d}u_{t}.

Proposition 2.3
.

For every
\alpha<\frac{1}{2}
,
{\mathbf{u}}\in\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}
a.s.

Proof.

By Sobolev embeddings, it is enough to show that
u\in\mathscr{W}^{\alpha,p}
a.s. for every

p>0
. We have that

\mathbb{E}|\left\langle{\nabla}\right\rangle^{\alpha}u(x)|^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\Big|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\left\langle{n}\right\rangle^{\alpha}\frac{g_{n}}{\sqrt{1+|n|^{4}}}e^{inx}\Big|^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\frac{\left\langle{n}\right\rangle^{2\alpha}}{1+|n|^{4}}\lesssim_{\alpha}1,

and similarly

\mathbb{E}|\left\langle{\nabla}\right\rangle^{-2+\alpha}u_{t}(x)|^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\Big|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\left\langle{n}\right\rangle^{-2+\alpha}h_{n}e^{inx}\Big|^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}}\left\langle{n}\right\rangle^{-4+2\alpha}\lesssim_{\alpha}1.

Therefore, by hypercontractivity, for
q>p
,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left\|{u}\right\|_{\mathscr{W}^{\alpha,p}}^{q}

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big(\int|\left\langle{\nabla}\right\rangle^{\alpha}u(x)|^{p}\mathrm{d}x+\int|\left\langle{\nabla}\right\rangle^{-2+\alpha}u_{t}(x)|^{p}\mathrm{d}x\Big)^{\frac{q}{p}}

\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\Big[\int|\left\langle{\nabla}\right\rangle^{\alpha}u(x)|^{q}\mathrm{d}x+\int|\left\langle{\nabla}\right\rangle^{-2+\alpha}u_{t}(x)|^{q}\mathrm{d}x\Big]

\displaystyle\lesssim\int(\mathbb{E}|\left\langle{\nabla}\right\rangle^{\alpha}u(x)|^{2})^{\frac{q}{2}}\mathrm{d}x+\int(\mathbb{E}|\left\langle{\nabla}\right\rangle^{-2+\alpha}u_{t}(x)|^{2})^{\frac{q}{2}}\mathrm{d}x

\displaystyle\lesssim_{\alpha}1,

and in particular
u\in\mathscr{W}^{\alpha,p}
a.s.
∎

Proposition 2.4
.

For every
\alpha<\frac{1}{2}
,
S(t){\mathbf{u}}\in C_{t}\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}
a.s. Moreover,

\sup_{t>0}\left\|{e^{\frac{t}{8}}S(t){\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{\mathscr{C}^{\alpha}}<+\infty

a.s. In particular,
{\mathbf{u}}\in X^{\alpha}
a.s.

Proof.

For a test function
\mathbf{f}
, we have that

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left\langle S(t){\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{f}\right\rangle\left\langle S(s){\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{f}\right\rangle=\left\langle\mathcal{L}S(t)^{\ast}\mathbf{f},S(s)^{\ast}\mathbf{f}\right\rangle=\left\langle S(s)\mathcal{L}\mathbf{f},S(t)\mathbf{f}\right\rangle=e^{-\frac{t+s}{2}}\overline{\gamma}(t,s),

where

\mathcal{L}\begin{pmatrix}f\\
f_{t}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}(1+\Delta^{2})^{-1}f\\
f_{t}\end{pmatrix}.

Therefore, we have
\overline{\gamma}(t,s)[\mathbf{f}]\lesssim\left\|{f}\right\|_{H^{-2}}^{2}+\left\|{f_{t}}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}
and
\Lip(\overline{\gamma}(\cdot,\cdot)[\mathbf{f}])\lesssim\left\|{f}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\left\|{f_{t}}\right\|_{H^{2}}^{2}
,
so we can conclude the proof exactly in the same way as in Proposition
2.2
.
∎

However, we are not interested in
\mu
, but in the
Gibbs measure

\rho
, which formally is given by

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\rho({\mathbf{u}})

\displaystyle=Z^{-1}\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int u^{4}-\frac{1}{2}\int u^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int(\Delta u)^{2}\Big)\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\int u_{t}^{2}\Big)\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}u_{t}

\displaystyle=Z^{-1}\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int u^{4}\Big)\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}),

where
Z
is the normalisation factor.

Proposition 2.5
.

The function
F({\mathbf{u}}):=\exp\big(-\frac{1}{4}\int u^{4}\big)
belongs to
L^{\infty}(\mu)
and
\left\|{F}\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\mu)}\leq 1
.
Moreover, if
F_{N}({\mathbf{u}}):=\exp\big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(P_{\leq N}u)^{4}\big)
, then
\left\|{F_{N}}\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\mu)}\leq 1
and

F_{N}\to F
in
L^{p}(\mu)
for every
1\leq p<+\infty
.

In particular, the probability measures

\rho_{N}:=Z_{N}^{-1}F_{N}\mu
,
\rho:=Z^{-1}F\mu
are well defined, absolutely continuous with respect to
\mu
, and, for every set
E
,
\rho_{N}(E)\to\rho(E)
.

Proof.

By Proposition
2.3
,
\int u^{4}<+\infty

\mu
-a.s., so
F,F_{N}
are well defined
\mu
-a.s.
Moreover, since
\int f^{4}\geq 0
for every
f
, we have that
F,F_{N}\leq 1
. Again by Proposition
2.3
,

P_{\leq N}u\to u
in
L^{4}
, so up to subsequences,
F_{N}\to F

\mu
-a.s., therefore
\int|F_{N}-F|^{p}\mathrm{d}\mu\to 0
by dominated convergence.
∎

3
Local and global well posedness

In this section, we will show local and global well posedness in
X^{\alpha}
for the equations (
4
), (
9
), relying onto the probabilistic estimates of the previous section and the
Da Prato-Debussche
trick.

Local well posedness will follow by a standard Banach fixed point argument. For global well posedness, following
[
8
]
we estimate an appropriate energy for the remainder
{\mathbf{v}}
, and we combine this argument with an integration by parts trick from
[
37
]
.

Proposition 3.2

(Continuity of the flow)
.

Let
{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}_{0})
solve (
18
) in an interval
[0,T^{*})
. Let
T<T^{*}
. Then there exists a neighbourhood

of
{\mathbf{u}}_{0}
such that

18

for every
\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{0}\in U\subseteq X^{\alpha}
and
\lim_{\left\|{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{0}-{\mathbf{u}}_{0}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}\to 0}{\mathbf{v}}(\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{0})={\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}_{0})

\lim_{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{0}\to{\mathbf{u}}_{0}}{\mathbf{v}}(\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{0})={\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}_{0})\end{gathered}\right\}\geq T^{*}.

, by definition of
\tau^{*}
we have that

\left\|{{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}_{0})(s)-{\mathbf{v}}(\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{0})(s)}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\to 0

as well and so

around
{\mathbf{u}}_{0}
,

\left\|{{\mathbf{v}}(\tilde{\mathbf{u}}_{0})}\right\|_{C([0,\tau^{*}+\varepsilon\wedge\tau];\mathcal{H}^{2})}\leq\left\|{{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}_{0})}\right\|_{C([0,\tau^{*}+\varepsilon\wedge\tau];\mathcal{H}^{2})}+1

which contradicts the maximality of
\tau^{*}
.
∎

Proof.

(
31
) follows just from Leibniz rule. In order to prove the estimate, notice that

\left\|{v}\right\|_{L^{4}}\lesssim E^{\frac{1}{4}}
, and
\left\|{v}\right\|_{H^{2}}\lesssim E^{\frac{1}{2}}
. Therefore, by
Hölder and fractional Leibniz respectively,

\left\{\begin{aligned} \left\|{v^{3}}\right\|_{L^{\frac{4}{3}}}&\lesssim E^{\frac{3}{4}}\\
\left\|{v^{3}}\right\|_{W^{2,1}}&\lesssim E.\end{aligned}\right.

Therefore, by interpolation (Gagliardo - Nirenberg), if
\frac{1}{p}=(1-\frac{\alpha}{2})+\frac{\alpha}{2}\cdot\frac{3}{4}=1-\frac{\alpha}{8}
, then

\left\|{v^{3}}\right\|_{W^{2-\alpha,p}}\lesssim E^{(1-\frac{\alpha}{2})+\frac{\alpha}{2}\cdot\frac{3}{4}}=E^{1-\frac{\alpha}{8}}
.

4
Invariance

The goal of this section is showing that the flow of (
4
) is a stochastic flow which satisfies the semigroup property, and proceed to prove that the measure
\rho
is invariant for the flow of (
4
).
Even if we will not use it explicitly in the following, the semigroup property ensures that the maps on Borel functions

F\mapsto P_{t}F:=\mathbb{E}[F(\Phi_{t}(\cdot;\xi))]

define a Markov semigroup, to which we can apply the usual theory for stationary measures.

Recall that, if
{\mathbf{u}}_{0}\in X^{\alpha}
, the flow
of (
4
) at time
t
with initial data

Proposition 4.1
.

The map
\Phi
satisfies the semigroup property, i.e. for every
F
measurable and bounded,

\mathbb{E}[F(\Phi_{t+s}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\xi))]=\mathbb{E}[F(\Phi_{s}(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\xi_{1});\xi_{2}))],

where
\xi_{1},\xi_{2}
are two independent copies of space-time white noise.

Proof.

Given
\xi_{1},\xi_{2}
independent copies of the white noise, let
\tilde{\xi}
be defined by

\langle{\tilde{\xi}},{\phi}\rangle:=\left\langle\mathbb{1}_{[0,t]}\xi_{1},\phi\right\rangle+\left\langle\mathbb{1}_{(t,+\infty)}\xi_{2}(\cdot-t),\phi\right\rangle

for every test function
\phi
.
It is easy to see that
\tilde{\xi}
satisfies the universal property

\mathbb{E}[|\langle{\tilde{\xi}},{f}\rangle|^{2}]=\left\|{f}\right\|_{L^{2}}^{2},

so it is a copy of space-time white noise. Moreover, from a direct computation,

\Phi_{s}(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\xi_{1}),\xi_{2})=\Phi_{t+s}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\tilde{\xi}),

and so for every
F
measurable and bounded,

\mathbb{E}[F(\Phi_{t+s}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\xi))]=\mathbb{E}[F(\Phi_{s}(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\xi_{1});\xi_{2}))].

∎

(34)

where
{\mathbf{v}}_{N}
solves (
10
). Then the measure

\mathrm{d}\rho_{N}({\mathbf{u}}):=\frac{1}{Z_{N}}\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(P_{\leq N}u)^{4}\Big)\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}})

(35)

is invariant for the the process associated to the flow
\Phi^{N}_{t}(\cdot;\xi)
, where
Z_{N}=\int\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(P_{\leq N}u)^{4}\Big)\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}})
(so that
\rho_{N}
is a probability measure).

Proof.

Let
\mathbf{X}
be a random variable with law
\mu
, independent from
\xi
. Invariance of (
35
) is equivalent to showing that

\mathbb{E}\Big[F(\Phi^{N}_{t}(\mathbf{X};\xi))\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(P_{\leq N}\pi_{1}\mathbf{X})^{4}\Big)\Big]=\mathbb{E}\Big[F(\mathbf{X})\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(P_{\leq N}\pi_{1}\mathbf{X})^{4}\Big)\Big]

for every
F:X^{\alpha}\to\mathbb{R}
continuous. Let
M\geq N
. By definition of
X^{\alpha}
, we have that

\lim_{M\to\infty}\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}-P_{M}{\mathbf{u}}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}=0
for every
u\in X^{\alpha^{\prime}}
,
\alpha^{\prime}>\alpha
. Therefore,
by Proposition
2.2
and Proposition
3.2
, one has that for every
t\geq 0
,

\lim_{M\to\infty}\left\|{\Phi^{N}_{t}(P_{M}\mathbf{X};P_{M}\xi)-\Phi_{t}^{N}(\mathbf{X};\xi)}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}}=0.

Therefore, by dominated convergence, it is enough to prove that

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[F(\Phi^{N}_{t}(P_{M}\mathbf{X};P_{M}\xi))\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(P_{\leq N}\pi_{1}\mathbf{X})^{4}\Big)\Big]

(36)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[F(P_{\leq M}\mathbf{X})\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(P_{\leq N}\pi_{1}\mathbf{X})^{4}\Big)\Big].

By (
34
), it is easy to check that
\mathbf{Y}=(Y,Y_{t})^{T}:=\Phi^{N}_{t}(\cdot;P_{M}\xi)
solves the SDE

\mathrm{d}\mathbf{Y}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
-(1+\Delta^{2})&-1\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{Y}-P_{\leq N}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
(P_{\leq N}Y)^{3}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}0\\
\sqrt{2}\mathrm{d}W_{M}\end{pmatrix},

where
\mathrm{d}W_{M}:=P_{M}\xi
is a space-time white noise on the finite dimensional space given by the image of the map
P_{M}
.
Therefore, if we show that the measure
\tilde{\rho}
defined on the image of
P_{M}
,

\mathrm{d}\tilde{\rho}(u):=\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(P_{\leq N}u)^{4}-\frac{1}{2}\int|u|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int|\Delta u|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int|u_{t}|^{2}\Big)\mathrm{d}u\mathrm{d}u_{t},

is invariant for the flow
\mathbf{Y}
, we get (
36
). Since
\mathbf{Y}
solves an SDE with smooth coefficients, this is true if and only if
\tilde{\rho}
solves
the Fokker-Planck equation

-\div\left[\Big(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
-(1+\Delta^{2})&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u\\
u_{t}\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}0\\
u^{3}\end{pmatrix}\Big)\tilde{\rho}(u,u_{t})\right]=0,

which can be shown through a direct computation.
∎

Corollary 4.3
.

The measure
\rho
is invariant by the flow of (
4
).

Proof.

By Corollary
3.5
, one has that for every
t>0
and every
{\mathbf{u}}_{0}\in X^{\alpha}
,
\Phi^{N}_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\xi)\to\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\xi)
in
X^{\alpha}
a.s.
Let
F:X^{\alpha}\to\mathbb{R}
be continuous and bounded. By dominated convergence and Proposition
4.2
, we have

\displaystyle\int\mathbb{E}\Big[F(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\xi))\Big]\mathrm{d}\rho({\mathbf{u}}_{0})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int\mathbb{E}\Big[F(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\xi))\Big]\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(u_{0})^{4}\Big)\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}_{0})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{N\to\infty}\int\mathbb{E}\Big[F(\Phi^{N}_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\xi))\Big]\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(P_{\leq N}\pi_{1}{\mathbf{u}}_{0})^{4}\Big)\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}_{0})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\lim_{N\to\infty}\int F({\mathbf{u}}_{0})\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(P_{\leq N}\pi_{1}{\mathbf{u}}_{0})^{4}\Big)\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}_{0})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int F({\mathbf{u}}_{0})\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{4}\int(\pi_{1}{\mathbf{u}}_{0})^{4}\Big)\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}_{0})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\int F({\mathbf{u}}_{0})\mathrm{d}\rho({\mathbf{u}}_{0}).

∎

5
Ergodicity

In this section, we proceed to show unique ergodicity for the flow
\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0};\xi)
of (
4
).
We recall that, as discussed in Section 1, the flow is naturally split as

{}{}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

\Psi({\mathbf{u}}):=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_{\{E_{t}+\mathcal{H}^{2}\}}(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}},\xi))]

. With the same

\Psi(\mathcal{H}^{2})=\{1\}
and

, and since

, we have that

.

5.1
Restricted Strong Feller property and irreducibility of the flow

In this subsection, we try to recover some weaker version of the strong Feller property for the flow
\Phi
. The
end result will be to prove the following lemma, which will be crucial for the proof of ergodicity:

Lemma 5.1
.

Let
\nu_{1},\nu_{2}
be two invariant measures (in the sense of (
2
)) such that
\nu_{1}\perp\nu_{2}
.
Then there exists some
V\subset X^{\alpha}
such that
\nu_{1}(V)=1
and
\nu_{2}(V+\mathcal{H}^{2})=0
.

In order to prove this, it is convenient to introduce the space
\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}=X^{\alpha}
equipped with the distance

d({\mathbf{u}}_{0},{\mathbf{u}}_{1})=\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}_{0}-{\mathbf{u}}_{1}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\wedge 1.

While
\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}
is a complete metric space and a vector space, it does not satisfy many of the usual hypotheses on ambient spaces:
it is
not
a topological vector space, it is
disconnected
, and it is
not
separable. Moreover,
the sigma-algebra
\mathscr{B}
of the Borel sets on
X^{\alpha}
, which is also the sigma-algebra we equip
\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}

with, does
not
coincide with the Borel sigma-algebra of
\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}
-
\mathscr{B}
is strictly smaller
2
2

2

Take
{\mathbf{u}}_{0}\in X^{\alpha}\setminus\mathcal{H}^{2}
, and let
E\subseteq\mathbb{R}
be not Borel. Then it is easy to see that
E{\mathbf{u}}_{0}:=\{\lambda{\mathbf{u}}_{0}|\lambda\in E\}
is
not
in
\mathscr{B}
, but it is
closed
in
\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}
.
.
However, in this topology, we can prove the strong Feller property.

Proposition 5.2

(Restricted strong Feller property)
.

The process associated to the flow
\Phi_{t}(\cdot;\xi)
of (
4
) defined on
\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}
has the strong Feller property, i.e. for every
t>0
, the function

P_{t}G({\mathbf{u}}):=\mathbb{E}[G(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}},\xi))]

is continuous as a function
\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}\to\mathbb{R}
for every
G:\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}\to\mathbb{R}
measurable and bounded.

We would like to point out that a phenomenon similar to the one described by this proposition, i.e. the fact that the strong Feller property holds only with respect to a stronger topology, has already been observed in the literature for other equations, for instance in
[
17
]
.

Before being able to prove Proposition
5.2
, we need the following (completely deterministic) lemma,
which will take the role of support theorems for
\xi

Since by Parseval
\left\|{w}\right\|_{H}=\left\|{\lambda_{n}\widehat{w}}\right\|_{l^{2}}
and
\left\|{w_{t}}\right\|_{L^{2}}=\left\|{\widehat{w}_{t}}\right\|_{l^{2}}
, the lemma is proven if we manage to prove that the quadratic form on
\mathbb{R}^{2}

B_{n}(x,y):=\int_{0}^{t}\Big|\sin(s\lambda_{n})x+\Big(\cos(s\lambda_{n})-\frac{\sin(s\lambda_{n})}{2\lambda_{n}}\Big)y\Big|^{2}\mathrm{d}s

satisfies
B_{n}\geq c_{n}\id
, with
c_{n}\geq\varepsilon>0
for every
n\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}
.
We have that
B_{n}>0
, since the integrand cannot be identically
0
for
(x,y)\neq(0,0)

(if the integrand is
0
, by evaluating it in
s=0
we get
y=0
, from which evaluating in almost any other
s
we get
x=0
). Therefore, it is enough to prove that
c_{n}\to c>0
as
|n|\to+\infty
. As
|n|\to+\infty
,

\lambda_{n}\to+\infty
as well, so

\displaystyle\lim_{n}

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\sin(s\lambda_{n})^{2}=\frac{t}{2},

\displaystyle\lim_{n}

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\cos(s\lambda_{n})^{2}=\frac{t}{2},

\displaystyle\lim_{n}

\displaystyle\phantom{\int_{0}^{t}}\frac{\sin(s\lambda_{n})}{2\lambda_{n}}=0,

\displaystyle\lim_{n}

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\sin(s\lambda_{n})\cos(s\lambda_{n})=0.

Hence,
B_{n}\to\frac{t}{2}\id
and so
c_{n}\to\frac{t}{2}>0
.
∎

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}_{t}(\xi))\mathcal{E}(T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}})].\end{multlined}

Up to changing
{\mathbf{v}}
outside of
E
, we can assume
\left\|{{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t)}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\leq C_{2}
.
Therefore, we have (using Girsanov again)

\displaystyle\phantom{=}\big|\mathbb{E}[G(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi))]-\mathbb{E}[G(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}},\xi))]\big|

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \leq\left\|{G}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}&\Big(2\mathbb{P}(\xi\in E^{c})+\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_{(E+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}})^{c}}\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t))]\\
&+\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_{(E+T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}})^{c}}\mathcal{E}(T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}})]\\
&+\mathbb{E}\big|\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t))-\mathcal{E}(T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}(({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0}),\xi;t))\big|\Big)\end{aligned}

\displaystyle=\left\|{G}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}(4\mathbb{P}(\xi\in E^{c})+\mathbb{E}\big|\mathcal{E}(T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t))-\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}),\xi;t)\big|)

Notice that, by Burkholder-Davis-Gundy inequality, for
h
in the form
h=T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{w}}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}
, with both
\left\|{{\mathbf{v}}}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}\leq C_{2}
and
\left\|{{\mathbf{w}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\leq C_{2}
,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\exp(p\left\langle h,\xi\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}})]

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k\geq 0}p^{k}\frac{1}{k!}\mathbb{E}[|\left\langle h,\xi\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}}|^{k}]

\displaystyle\leq 1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p^{k}C^{k}\frac{k^{\frac{k}{2}}}{k!}\big(\left\|{T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{w}}}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{k}+\mathbb{E}[\left\|{\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{k}]\big)

\displaystyle\leq 1+\Psi_{1}(\left\|{{\mathbf{w}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}})\left\|{{\mathbf{w}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}+\Psi_{2}(C_{2})\mathbb{E}[\left\|{\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2}]^{\frac{1}{2}},

\displaystyle\leq\Psi(C_{2}).

where
\Psi_{1},\Psi_{2},\Psi
are monotone analytic functions with infinite radius of convergence.
With the same computation, we get

\mathbb{E}[\big(\exp(p\left\langle h,\xi\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}})-1\big)^{n}]\leq\Psi_{3,n}(C_{2})(\left\|{{\mathbf{w}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}+\mathbb{E}[\left\|{\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2}]^{\frac{1}{2}})\lesssim_{n,C_{2}}\mathbb{E}[\left\|{h}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2}]^{\frac{1}{2}}.

Therefore, by continuity of the flow of (
4
) in the initial data, for
\left\|{{\mathbf{v}}_{0}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\ll 1
, we have that

\displaystyle\phantom{=}\mathbb{E}\big|\mathcal{E}(T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t))-\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}),\xi;t)\big|

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} =&\mathbb{E}\Big[\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\left\|{\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t)}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2}+\left\langle\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t),\xi\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}}\Big)\\
&\begin{multlined}\times\Big(\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}(\left\|{T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t)}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2}-\left\|{\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t)}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2})\\
+\left\langle T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t)-\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t),\xi\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}}\Big)-1\Big)\Big]\end{multlined}\\
=&\mathbb{E}\Big[\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\left\|{\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t)}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2}+\left\langle\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t),\xi\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}}\Big)\\
&\resizebox{21931650}{}{$\displaystyle\begin{multlined}\times\Big(\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}(\left\|{T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t)}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2}-\left\|{\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t)}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2})\Big)-1\Big)\\
\times\exp\Big(\left\langle T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t)-\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t),\xi\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}}\Big)\end{multlined}$}\\
&\phantom{\times\Big(}\,+\exp\Big(\left\langle T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t)-\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t),\xi\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}}\Big)-1\Big)\Big]\end{aligned}

\displaystyle\leq\Big[\mathbb{E}\exp\Big(2\left\langle\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t),\xi\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}}\Big)\Big]^{\frac{1}{2}}

\displaystyle\times\Big[\Big(\mathbb{E}\Big(\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}(\left\|{T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t)}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2}-\left\|{\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t)}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2})\Big)-1\Big)^{4}\Big)^{\frac{1}{4}}

\displaystyle\phantom{\leq\times\Big[}\times\Big(\mathbb{E}\exp\Big(4\left\langle T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t)-\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t),\xi\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}}\Big)\Big)^{\frac{1}{4}}

\displaystyle\phantom{\leq\times\Big[}+\resizebox{20122815}{}{$\displaystyle\Big(\mathbb{E}\Big(\exp\Big(\left\langle T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t)-\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t),\xi\right\rangle_{L^{2}_{t,x}}\Big)-1\Big)^{2}\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big]$}

\displaystyle\lesssim_{C_{2}}[\mathbb{E}\left\|{T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t)-\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}},\xi;t)}\right\|_{L^{2}_{t,x}}^{2}]^{\frac{1}{2}},

which is converging to
0
as
\left\|{{\mathbf{v}}_{0}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\to 0
because of dominated convergence. Therefore,

\displaystyle\limsup_{\left\|{v_{0}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\to 0}\big|\mathbb{E}[G(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi))]-\mathbb{E}[G(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}},\xi))]\big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\limsup_{\left\|{v_{0}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\to 0}\left\|{G}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}\left(\begin{multlined}4\mathbb{P}(\xi\in E^{c})\\
+\mathbb{E}\big|\mathcal{E}(T_{t}S(t){\mathbf{v}}_{0}+\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi;t))-\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T}_{t}{\mathbf{v}}({\mathbf{u}}),\xi;t)\big|\end{multlined}\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 4\left\|{G}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}\mathbb{P}(\xi\in E^{c}).

Since the left-hand-side does not depend on
C_{1}
, we can send
C_{1}\to\infty
, and we obtain that

\lim_{\left\|{v_{0}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\to 0}\big|\mathbb{E}[G(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}+{\mathbf{v}}_{0},\xi))]-\mathbb{E}[G(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}},\xi))]\big|=0,

i.e.
\mathbb{E}[G(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}},\xi))]
is continuous in
{\mathbf{u}}
in the
\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}
topology.
∎

While the topology of
\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}
does not allow to extend many common consequences of the strong Feller property,
we still have the following generalisation of the disjoint supports property.

Corollary 5.4
.

Let
\nu_{1}\perp\nu_{2}
be two invariant measures. Then there exists a measurable
open set
V_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}
such that
\nu_{1}(V_{0})=1
and
\nu_{2}(V_{0})=0
.

Proof.

Let
S_{1}\subset\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}
be a measurable set with
\nu_{1}(S_{1})=1
,
\nu_{2}(S_{1})=0
. Recall that a set is measurable if and only if it is Borel in
X^{\alpha}
. Consider the function

\Psi({\mathbf{u}}):=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_{S_{1}}(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}},\xi))].

By the Proposition
5.2
,
\Psi:\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}\to\mathbb{R}
is continuous. Moreover, since
S_{1}
is a Borel set in
X^{\alpha}
,
\Psi
is also measurable.
By invariance of
\nu_{j}
,
\Psi=1

\nu_{1}
-a.s. and
\Psi=0

\nu_{2}
-a.s. Let
V_{0}:=\{\Psi>\frac{1}{2}\}
. We have that
V_{0}\subset\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}
is open
by continuity of
\Psi
, it is measurable since
\Psi
is measurable,

\nu_{1}(V_{0})\geq\nu_{1}(\{\Psi=1\})=1

and

\nu_{2}(V_{0})\leq\nu_{2}(\{\Psi\neq 0\})=0.

∎

Lemma 5.5

(Irreducibility)
.

Suppose that
\nu
is invariant for the flow of (
4
), and let
E\subset X^{\alpha}
such that
\nu(E)=0
.
Then for every
{\mathbf{w}}\in\mathcal{H}^{2}
,
\nu(E+{\mathbf{w}})=0
.

X^{\alpha}
is a Polish space, by inner regularity of

Proof of Lemma
5.1
.

Let
\nu_{1}\perp\nu_{2}
be two invariant measures, let
V=V_{0}
be the set given by Corollary
5.4
, and let
\{{\mathbf{w}}_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}
be a countable dense subset of
\mathcal{H}^{2}
. We have that, by definition,

\nu_{1}(V)=1
and
\nu_{2}(V)=0
. By Lemma
5.5
,
\nu_{2}(V+{\mathbf{w}}_{n})=0
for
every
{\mathbf{w}}_{n}
. Therefore,
\nu_{2}(\bigcup_{n}(V+{\mathbf{w}}_{n}))=0
. Moreover, since
V
is open in
\mathcal{X}^{\alpha}
,
we have that
\bigcup_{n}(V+{\mathbf{w}}_{n})=V+\mathcal{H}^{2}
. Therefore,
\nu_{2}(V+\mathcal{H}^{2})=0
.
∎

5.2

\rho

linear

(37)

Lemma 5.6
.

The measure
\mu
is the only invariant measure for (
37

{\mathbf{u}}_{0}\in X^{\alpha}

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}_{t}(\xi))]\big|

\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}[\min(\Lip(F)\left\|{S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{0}-S(t){\mathbf{u}}_{1}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}},\left\|{F}\right\|_{L^{\infty}})]

\displaystyle\leq\min(e^{-\frac{t}{8}}\Lip(F)\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}_{0}-{\mathbf{u}}_{1}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}},\left\|{F}\right\|_{L^{\infty}})

Therefore by invariance of
\mu
, we have that

\displaystyle\Big|\mathbb{E}[F(L(t){\mathbf{u}}_{0})]-\int F({\mathbf{u}}_{1})\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}_{1})\Big|

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Big|\int\big(\mathbb{E}[F(L(t){\mathbf{u}}_{0})-\mathbb{E}[F(L(t){\mathbf{u}}_{1})]\big)\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}_{1})\Big|

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\int\min(e^{-\frac{t}{8}}\Lip(F)\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}_{0}-{\mathbf{u}}_{1}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}},\left\|{F}\right\|_{L^{\infty}})\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}_{1}),

which is converging to
0
by dominated convergence. Since Lipschitz functions are dense in the set of continuous functions, this implies
that the law of
L(t){\mathbf{u}}_{0}
is weakly converging to
\mu
. Similarly, if
\nu
is another invariant measure,

\displaystyle\phantom{=}\Big|\int F({\mathbf{u}}_{0})\mathrm{d}\nu({\mathbf{u}}_{0})-\int F({\mathbf{u}}_{1})\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}_{1})\Big|

\displaystyle=\Big|\iint\big(\mathbb{E}[F(L(t){\mathbf{u}}_{0})-\mathbb{E}[F(L(t){\mathbf{u}}_{1})]\big)\mathrm{d}\nu({\mathbf{u}}_{0})\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}_{1})\Big|

\displaystyle\leq\iint\min(e^{-\frac{t}{8}}\Lip(F)\left\|{{\mathbf{u}}_{0}-{\mathbf{u}}_{1}}\right\|_{X^{\alpha}},\left\|{F}\right\|_{L^{\infty}})\mathrm{d}\nu({\mathbf{u}}_{0})\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}_{1}),

which is converging to
0
by dominated convergence. Since the left hand side does not depend on
t
, one gets that
\int F({\mathbf{u}}_{0})\mathrm{d}\nu({\mathbf{u}}_{0})=\int F({\mathbf{u}}_{1})\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}}_{1})
for every
F
Lipschitz, so
\mu=\nu
.
∎

Consider the (algebraic) projection
\pi:X^{\alpha}\to X^{\alpha}/\mathcal{H}^{2}
. While the quotient space does
not have a sensible topology, we can define the quotient sigma-algebra,

\mathcal{A}:=\{F\subseteq X^{\alpha}/\mathcal{H}^{2}\text{ s.t. }\pi^{-1}(F)\subseteq X^{\alpha}\text{ Borel}\},

which corresponds to the finest
\sigma
-algebra that makes the map
\pi
measurable. While this will not be relevant in the following, we can see that
\mathcal{A}
is
relatively rich: if
E\subset X^{\alpha}
is closed and
B
is the closed unit ball in
\mathcal{H}^{2}
, since
B
is compact in
X^{\alpha}
,

E+nB
is closed for every
n
, so
E+\mathcal{H}^{2}=\bigcup_{n}E+nB
is Borel. Therefore,
\pi(E)\in\mathcal{A}
.

Since
S(t)
maps
\mathcal{H}^{2}
into itself, is it easy to see that if
\pi({\mathbf{u}})=\pi({\mathbf{v}})
, then
\pi(L(t){\mathbf{u}})=\pi(L(t){\mathbf{v}})
.
Therefore,
\pi(L(t){\mathbf{u}})
is a function of
\pi({\mathbf{u}})
, and we define

\overline{L}(t)\pi({\mathbf{u}}):=\pi(L(t){\mathbf{u}}).

Proposition 5.7
.

The measure
\pi_{\sharp}(\mu)
is ergodic for the process associated to
\overline{L}(t):X^{\alpha}/\mathcal{H}^{2}\to X^{\alpha}/\mathcal{H}^{2}
.

Proof.

If
G:X^{\alpha}/\mathcal{H}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}
is a bounded measurable function, then by invariance of
\mu
,

\displaystyle\int\mathbb{E}[G(\overline{L}(t)x)]\mathrm{d}\pi_{\sharp}\mu(x)

\displaystyle=\int\mathbb{E}[G(\overline{L}(t)\pi({\mathbf{u}}))]\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}})

(39)

\displaystyle=\int\mathbb{E}[G(\pi(L(t){\mathbf{u}}))]\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}})

\displaystyle=\int G(\pi({\mathbf{u}}))\mathrm{d}\mu({\mathbf{u}})

\displaystyle=\int G(x)\mathrm{d}\pi_{\sharp}\mu(x),

so
\pi_{\sharp}\mu
is invariant.

Let now
G
be a function such that
\mathbb{E}[G(\overline{L}(t)x)]=G(x)
for
\pi_{\sharp}\mu
-a.e.
x~{\!\in\!}~X^{\alpha}/\mathcal{H}^{2}
​.
Then

\mathbb{E}[G\circ\pi(L(t){\mathbf{u}})]\mathbb{E}[G(\pi(L(t){\mathbf{u}}))]=E[G(\overline{L}(t)\pi({\mathbf{u}}))]=G(\pi({\mathbf{u}})),

so
G\circ\pi
is
\mu
-a.s. constant by ergodicity of
\mu
. Therefore,
G
is
\pi_{\sharp}\mu
-a.s. constant,
so
\pi_{\sharp}\mu
is ergodic.
∎

Remark 5.8
.

We can see
\mu
as the law of the random variable
{\mathbf{u}}
defined in (
15
).
In this way, for every
E\subset X^{\alpha}
, by definition
\mu(E)=\mathbb{P}(\{{\mathbf{u}}\in E\})
. If
E=E+\mathcal{H}^{2}
, then
the event
\{{\mathbf{u}}\in E\}
is independent from
\{g_{n},h_{n}||n|<N\}
for every
N
, since
\mathcal{H}^{2}
contains every
function with finite Fourier support. Therefore,
E\in\bigcap_{N}\sigma(g_{n},h_{n}||n|\geq N)
.
By Kolmogorov’s 0-1 theorem, this implies that
\mu(E)=0
or
\mu(E)=1
.

Since by definition

\pi_{\sharp}\mu(F)=\mu(\pi^{-1}(F))
and
\pi^{-1}(F)=\pi^{-1}(F)+\mathcal{H}^{2}
, then
for
every
set
F\in\mathcal{A}
we have
\pi_{\sharp}\mu(F)\in\{0,1\}
, therefore trivially any invariant set has
measure
0
or
1
, hence the measure
\pi_{\sharp}\mu
is ergodic.

Proposition 5.9
.

Let
\nu
be an invariant measure for the flow of (
4
) such that
\pi_{\sharp}\nu\ll\pi_{\sharp}\mu
. Then
\nu=\rho
.
5
5

5

Notice that since
\rho\ll\mu
, then
\pi_{\sharp}\rho\ll\pi_{\sharp}\mu
.

Proof.

Suppose by contradiction that
\nu\neq\rho
. Let

\displaystyle\rho_{1}=\frac{1}{(\rho-\nu)_{+}(X^{\alpha})}(\rho-\nu)_{+}

\displaystyle\rho_{2}=\frac{1}{(\nu-\rho)_{+}(X^{\alpha})}(\nu-\rho)_{+}.

Since
\rho,\nu
are invariant, it is easy to see that
\rho_{1},\rho_{2}
are both invariant probabilities.
Moreover,
\rho_{1}\perp\rho_{2}
, and
\rho_{j}\ll\rho+\nu
, so
\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}\ll\pi_{\sharp}\rho+\pi_{\sharp}\nu\ll\pi_{\sharp}\mu
.

Proceeding as for (
39
), and using (
38
), we have

\displaystyle\int\mathbb{E}[G(\overline{L}(t)x)]\mathrm{d}\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}(x)

\displaystyle=\int\mathbb{E}[G(\overline{L}(t)\pi({\mathbf{u}}))]\mathrm{d}\rho_{j}({\mathbf{u}})

\displaystyle=\int\mathbb{E}[G(\pi(\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}};\xi)))]\mathrm{d}\rho_{j}({\mathbf{u}})

\displaystyle=\int G(\pi({\mathbf{u}}))\mathrm{d}\rho_{j}({\mathbf{u}})

\displaystyle=\int G(x)\mathrm{d}\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}(x),

therefore
\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}
is invariant. Moreover, since
\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}\ll\pi_{\sharp}\mu
, by invariance of
\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}
and ergodicity of
\pi_{\sharp}\mu
,
we must have
\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}=\pi_{\sharp}\mu
.
Let now
V
be the set given by Lemma
5.1
, i.e.
\rho_{1}(V)=1
,
\rho_{2}(V+\mathcal{H}^{2})=0
.
We have

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\rho_{2}(V+\mathcal{H}^{2})=\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{2}(\pi(V+\mathcal{H}^{2}))=\pi_{\sharp}\mu(\pi(V+\mathcal{H}^{2}))

\displaystyle=\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{1}(\pi(V+\mathcal{H}^{2}))=\rho_{1}(V+\mathcal{H}^{2})\geq\rho_{1}(V)=1,

contradiction.
∎

Remark 5.10
.

Using Remark
5.8
, it is possible to show
\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}=\pi_{\sharp}\mu
without using the ergodicity of

\pi_{\sharp}\mu
. We have indeed that
\rho_{j}\ll\mu
implies
\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}\ll\pi_{\sharp}\mu
. Let

E
be any set with
\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}(E)>0
. Then by absolute continuity,

\pi_{\sharp}\mu(E)>0
as well, and by Remark
5.8
,
\pi_{\sharp}\mu(E)=1\geq\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}(E)
.
Therefore
\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}\leq\pi_{\sharp}\mu
, and since they are both probabilities, we must have

\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}=\pi_{\sharp}\mu
.

Corollary 5.11
.

The measure
\rho
is ergodic for the Markov process associated to the flow
\Phi_{t}(\cdot,\xi):X^{\alpha}\to X^{\alpha}
of (
4
).

Proof.

Let
\nu\ll\rho
,
\nu
invariant. We have that
\pi_{\sharp}\nu\ll\pi_{\sharp}\rho\ll\pi_{\sharp}\mu
. Hence, by Proposition
5.9
,
\nu=\rho
. Therefore,
\rho
is ergodic.
∎

We conclude this section by proving unique ergodicity for the measure
\rho
. This will be the only part of this
paper for which we require the good long-time estimates for the flow given by (
24
) (up to this
point, whenever we used Corollary
3.5
, we needed just the qualitative result of global existence and

time-dependent
bounds on the growth of the solution).

In particular, we will prove the following version of Birkhoff’s theorem for this process, which in particular implies
Theorem
1.1
.

, we have that also the law of
{\mathbf{v}}
is tight; more precisely, there exists constants
c_{\varepsilon}
such that

\mathbb{P}(\{\left\|{{\mathbf{v}}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\leq c_{\varepsilon}\})\geq 1-\varepsilon
, uniformly in
t
.
Therefore,

\mathbb{P}(\big\{\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0},\xi)\in K_{\varepsilon}+\{\left\|{\cdot}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}}\leq c_{\varepsilon}\}\big\})\geq 1-2\varepsilon,

so also the law of
\Phi_{t}({\mathbf{u}}_{0},\xi)
is tight. By averaging in time, we obtain that also the sequence
\rho_{t}
is. Hence it is enough to prove that
every weak limit point
\overline{\rho}
of
\rho_{t}
satisfies
\overline{\rho}=\rho
. Notice that, by definition,
\overline{\rho}
is invariant.

, so
(\pi_{1})_{\sharp}\nu=\mu
. Recall
the projection
\pi:X^{\alpha}\to X^{\alpha}/\mathcal{H}^{2}
. On
X^{\alpha}\times\mathcal{H}^{2}
, we have that

\pi\circ\mathfrak{S}=\pi\circ\pi_{1}
. Therefore, since
\nu
is concentrated on
X^{\alpha}\times\mathcal{H}^{2}
,

\pi_{\sharp}\overline{\rho}=\pi_{\sharp}\mathfrak{S}_{\sharp}\nu=\pi_{\sharp}(\pi_{1})_{\sharp}\nu=\pi_{\sharp}\mu.

Hence, by Proposition (
5.9
), we get
\overline{\rho}=\rho
.
∎

Remark 5.13
.

If we could improve Proposition
5.7

to
unique
ergodicity for the measure

\pi_{\sharp}\mu
, we would automatically improve the result of
Corollary
5.11
to
unique

ergodicity, without using at all the long time estimates for the growth of
{\mathbf{v}}
. Indeed, in the proof of Proposition

5.9
, the only point in which we used the condition
\rho_{j}\ll\rho
was for showing that

\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}=\pi_{\sharp}\mu
. If we knew that the measure
\pi_{\sharp}\mu
was uniquely ergodic, then

\pi_{\sharp}\rho_{j}=\pi_{\sharp}\mu
will follow automatically from invariance, without the need for the extra condition
\rho_{j}\ll\rho
.
